Abstract 20 
Cell type annotation remains a critical bottleneck, with current methods often inaccurate and requiring 21 
extensive manual validation, particularly in disease contexts. While large language models (LLMs) show 22 
promise, they can be unreliable due to hallucinations. We developed CyteType, a multi-agent framework that 23 
generates competing hypotheses grounded in full expression data and study context, validates against external 24 
databases, and iteratively self -evaluates. Comprehensive b enchmarking demonstrates that CyteType 25 
substantially outperforms reference-based and LLM-based methods, with self-generated confidence scores 26

Main text 7 
Single-cell RNA sequencing datasets now routinely contain millions of cells  1,2. As computational methods 8 
are becoming increasingly  more efficient, the bottleneck has shifted from data analysis to biological 9 
interpretation 3,4, particularly in identifying cell type identities of clusters. Cell type annotation remains most 10 
challenging in disease contexts 5,6, and current reference-based classifiers trained on healthy tissue exhibit an 11 
accuracy drop of 15-30% when applied to disease samples 7, missing rare cell types in approximately 20% of 12 
cases. Manual annotation can lead to superior results over automated methods but is time-consuming and 13 
shows 25% inter-annotator variability 8. Additionally, current methods provide only cell type labels without 14 
justification or caveats 9, limiting result interpretability. Large language models (LLMs) have shown potential 15 
for cell type annotation, with GPT-4 achieving 75% agreement with expert annotations 10. However, existing 16 
LLM approaches have significant limitations: they process only top marker genes rather than full expression 17 
profiles, rely on static knowledge from pretraining data 11, and  lack mechanisms to validate predictions 18 
against external databases or quantify uncertainty.  19 
We developed CyteType, a multi -agent framework  that addresses these limitations through three key 20 
innovations (Figure 1A). First, CyteType implements hypothesis-driven reasoning, systematically testing 21 
competing cell type interpretations against full expression profiles, pathway enrichment, and study context 22 
to mimic expert annotation workflows . Second, it validates predictions by simulating an expert panel that 23 
performs automated reference checking against marker databases  12–14 . Third, it provides comprehensive 24 
biological context  by connecting annotations to current literature, disease associations , and therapeutic 25

Rigorous benchmarking of cell type prediction algorithms has proven challenging due to the free-text nature 1 
of cell type labels. To address this, we developed CyteOnto, a semantic similarity framework that maps cell 2 
type labels to Cell Ontology terms using text embeddings of LLM -augmented descriptions (Figure 1B). 3 
Unlike string-matching or graph-based methods that fail to capture semantic relationships, CyteOnto maps 4 
predicted and ground -truth (authors annotation) to their nearest Cell Ontology terms in embedding space, 5 
then quantifies normalized distances between these terms to derive a kernel-induced similarity score ranging 6 
from 0 to 1. Validation against curated test cases demonstrated that CyteOnto preserves biological meaning, 7 
maintains monotonic similarity score decay across cell type hierarchies, and outperforms traditional ontology 8 
distance metrics (Supplementary Information 1). This framework enabled quantitative comparison of 9 
CyteType against existing methods using similarity scores rather than exact or fuzzy label matching. 10 
We evaluated CyteType on four benchmark datasets  15–18 spanning 205 clusters , across diverse biological 11 
contexts (Figure 1B), using author provided annotations as ground truth proxy. To measure accuracy of 12 
predicted cell types from each benchmarked methods, we used CyteOnto similarity scores against the ground 13 
truth proxies. To isolate architectural benefits of CyteType from underlying LLM capabilities, we compared 14 
CyteType against GPTCellType  10 using identical LLM (GPT -5), alongside established reference -based 15 
methods: CellTypist 18 and SingleR 19. Using identical models (GPT-5), CyteType significantly outperformed 16 
GPTCellType with 388.52% higher similarity score across four datasets (z = 8.04, p < .001, Tukey-adjusted), 17 
demonstrating that structured hypothesis testing and evidence collection improve upon direct LLM prompting 18 
(Figure 1C). This performance-gain demonstrates that CyteType's architectural innovations provide value 19 
independent of underlying LLM capabilities. CyteType’s median similarity score also exceeded those from 20 
reference-based methods, CellTypist (z = 8.15, p < .001) and SingleR (z = 8.36, p < .001), with performance 21 
gains consistent across diverse biological contexts  but most pronounced in multi tissue datasets. CyteType 22 
showed 267.9% and 100.67% higher average similarity score over CellTypist and SingleR, respectively. One 23 
notable exception was CellTypist's near-perfect (similarity score: median: 1.0, mean: 0.8 ) performance on 24 
the immune cell atlas dataset, where author labels were generated using CellTypist itself, serving as a positive 25 
control for CyteOnto's similarity scoring.  Hence, CyteType outperformed existing cell annotation methods 26

To assess robustness of CyteType’s architecture, we benchmarked 16 LLMs spanning closed -weight (e.g. 4 
GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro)  and open-weight models (DeepSeek R1 21, Qwen3 Thinking) 5 
(Figure 1C). Closed-weight models achieved the highest mean similarity score, while open-weight models 6 
showed modest but significant ly decreased  (b = -0.035, SE = 0.011, p < .001) mean score yet still 7 
outperformed traditional methods. Notably, LLMs with built-in chain-of-thought reasoning demonstrated no 8 
significant advantage (b = 0.014, SE = 0.011, t(3977), p = 0.22) over standard models, suggesting CyteType's 9 
structured workflow supersedes model-native reasoning capabilities. This finding has practical implications: 10 
researchers can select models based on cost and privacy requirements without sacrificing the benefits of 11 
CyteType's architecture. Closed-weight models (GPT -5, Claude Sonnet 4) maximize accuracy for critical 12 
applications, while open-weight models (Kimi K2 20, Deepseek R1) achieve 95% of peak performance at low 13 
cost, suitable for exploratory analysis or budget-constrained settings (Supplementary Information 2).  14 
Having established CyteType’s performance and robustness  across LLMs, we next evaluated whether its 15 
predictions can be trusted and systematically interpreted. CyteType's Reviewer agent (Figure 1A) generates 16 
calibrated confidence scores and heterogeneity flags that enable targeted expert review. High -confidence 17 
annotations were significantly more likely to have higher similarity score than those with low-confidence (F 18 
= 23.88, p < .001), while heterogeneous clusters showed significantly lower similarity score against author 19 
labels (F = 8.45, p < .01). Across repeated runs, median majority agreement exceeded 80% for all LLMs, 20 
with consensus Cell Ontology labels achieved for >70% of clusters.  Both r eviewer confidence and 21 
heterogeneity flags predicted similarity scores even after accounting for LLM choice (likelihood ratio test: χ² 22 
= 42.06, df = 16, p < .001 and χ² = 35.44, df = 16, p < .01, respectively). These metrics create an interpretable 23 
“trust layer”  that existing annotation methods lack, transforming cell type annotation from a black -box 24 
classification into a transparent process with quantified uncertainty. 25

Finally, we evaluated whether CyteType’s evidence-based framework extends beyond accurate classification 1 
to enable refinement of existing data potentially leading to novel discoveries . Applying CyteType to 977 2 
clusters across 20 datasets revealed systematic patterns . Rather than simply validating existing annotations, 3 
CyteType added value across all scenarios : 41% of clusters received functional enhancement (e.g., adding 4 
cell state information), 29% underwent refinement to specific subtypes, and 30% required major reannotation 5 
(Supplementary Information 3) . Importantly, t his distribution demonstrates that CyteType functions not 6 
merely as a classifier but as a discovery tool , uncovering biological context missed by reference -based 7 
methods. Annotations mapped to 327 unique Cell Ontology terms with high diversity (no term exceeding 8 
2.5% frequency) and identified 116 distinct cell states, with activation (37%) and maturation (16%) most 9 
prevalent. Predicted heterogeneity strongly correlated with lower confidence (Pearson's correlation 10 
coefficient: r = -0.79, p < .001), validating the system's ability to flag mixed populations. High -confidence 11 
discrepancies occurred predominantly in  disease contexts where reference methods historically 12 
underperform, suggesting CyteType uncovers biologically meaningful refinements . For example, in the 13 
diabetic kidney disease atlas author denominated parietal epithelial cells  and leukocytes were relabelled 14 
injured proximal tubule cell (ALDH1A2+, CFH+, VCAM1+)  and T cell (activated CD45+DOCK2+ pro -15 
inflammatory) respectively. 16 
CyteType is available as Python  (AnnData 22 compatible) and R packages (CyteTypeR for Seurat  23 17 
compatibility) and generates  comprehensive reports that integrate directly into existing workflows. Cell type 18 
annotations are returned  into AnnData/Seurat objects along with Cell Ontology terms for downstream 19 
analysis and data integration. Interactive HTML reports provide detailed marker justification, pathway 20 
enrichment, literature evidence, and disease associations, with embedded chat functionality enabling iterative 21 
refinement and hypothesis exploration. 22

identification from classification into evidence -based characterization. While reference -based methods 25 
constrain predictions to previously characterized cell types and degrade under domain shift, and transformer-26

for novel contexts, CyteType's hypothesis-testing framework discovers cell states and rare populations with 2

METHODS 6 
CyteType Architecture and Implementation 7 
CyteType is a multi-agent system designed to automate the rigorous scientific reasoning process for cell type 8 
annotation. The CyteType architecture breaks the annotation task into five distinct, collaborative agents. The 9 
Contextualizer agent sets up the context by inferring organism, tissue, and pathway context before 10 
annotation and establishing biological ground truth. The Annotator agent employs a hypothesis -driven 11 
framework, generating and systematically testing multiple biological interpretations for each cell cluster to 12 
facilitate evidence-based identification. The Reviewer agent provides a critical validation, using a simulated 13 
panel of domain experts and external reference databases to assess annotation confidence and detect cellular 14 
heterogeneity. The Literature & Clinical Relevance  agent connects the findings to PubMed literature, 15 
Disease Ontology, and Drug Ontology. Finally, the Summarizer agent synthesizes the results into a coherent, 16 
study-wide biological narrative, which can be viewed as a report on a browser. Additionally, the Chat agent 17 
and user-triggered reannotations with feedback enable users to introspect agentic reasoning, query data, and 18 
update annotations. 19

CyteType is designed as a resilient and scalable API -driven service that integrates multiple specialized AI 2 
agents, external biological databases, and large language models (LLMs) to perform end -to-end cell type 3 
annotation. 4 
Data Ingestion and Preparation 5 
The workflow begins with data ingestion with standard single-cell data formats like AnnData objects (.h5ad) 6 
and Seurat ( .RDS), as well as direct data submission via API calls. Along with the expression data, users 7 
provide essential study context (e.g., species, tissue source, experimental design). This information is 8 
consolidated into an internal query -ready database that stores the expression percentages for each gene in 9 
each cluster, top marker genes for each cluster, and associated percentages across metadata categories for 10 
efficient access by the agentic system. 11

Integration with LLMs and External Databases 1 
The agents are powered by a suite of LLMs (e.g., GPT -5, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, etc.) equipped 2 
with function -calling abilities. This allows the agents to interact programmatically with a wide array of 3 
external biological databases, which are available as callable “tools.” These resources include ontologies 4 
(Cell Ontology, Gene Ontology), literature databases (PubMed), and specialized molecular databases (GTEx, 5 
CellGuide, Drug Ontology), ensuring that all reasoning is grounded in established scientific knowledge. Tool 6 
usage budgets are enforced per agent with automatic prompt constraints when approaching limits. 7 
System Outputs and Integration  8 
CyteType delivers its results through multiple formats to suit different user needs. A structured JSON output 9 
provides granular annotations and ontology IDs for computational use. A comprehensive HTML report offers 10 
a user-friendly view of the results, including an interface for human-in-the-loop feedback and re-annotation 11 
via a chat portal, enabling interactive, human -led investigation of the data. The final annotations can be 12 
integrated back into the original AnnData or Seurat objects, allowing researchers to proceed with familiar 13 
downstream analysis and visualization tools. This entire workflow is deployed on a scalable cloud 14 
infrastructure, enabling the parallel processing of hundreds of clusters simultaneously and making it suitable 15 
for large-scale single-cell transcriptomic studies. 16 
 17 
Scalable Processing 18 
The system implements concurrent cluster processing with configurable parallelism (default 20 clusters, 19 
scalable to hundreds simultaneously). Processing time averages 5-10 minutes per cluster  but can vary 20 
depending on speed of chosen LLM and model provider’s inference speed, and the number of self-iterations, 21 
consuming between 4 00,000 and 600,000  tokens per cluster. Pathway enrichment analysis executes via 22 
distributed compute functions with horizontal scaling and isolation. 23

CyteType employs multi -provider rotation with primary/secondary/fallback selection and preflight 1 
validation. Agent execution implements unified retry policies with exponential backoff (5s → 10s → 30±30s 2 
→ 60±60s) for HTTP  and model output structure validation errors . The system supports deployment via 3 
cloud APIs (OpenRouter, AWS Bedrock) or local ly hosted Ollama models with configurable timeout and 4 
scaling parameters. Per-call cycling ensures diversity and resilience while usage limits prevent cost overruns. 5

Dataset Selection 7 
Four benchmark datasets were selected to span diverse biological contexts: HypoMap (developing mouse 8 
brain, 66 clusters), Immune Cell Atlas (human immune cells, 45 clusters), GTEx v9 (cross -tissue human 9 
atlas, 74 clusters), and Mouse Pancreatic Cell Atlas (pancreatic tissue, 20 clusters). Datasets were down 10 
sampled to reduce computational requirements while preserving cellular diversity (Table SI-3-1, with down 11 
sampling notebooks available at 12

Atlas), and tissue-specific models (GTEx v9). 21

matched testing contexts: HumanPrimaryCellAtlasData (Immune Cell Atlas and GTEx v9) and 23 
MouseRNAseqData (Mouse Pancreatic Cell Atlas and HypoMap). 24

Multi-LLM Benchmark 8 
Sixteen LLMs were evaluated, meeting selection criteria: context window >32,000 tokens, input cost <$5 per 9 
million tokens, accessible via OpenRouter, tool -use capabilities, and Graduate -level Google -proof Q&A 10

were compared against original author labels using CyteOnto semantic similarity, categorized as high (66.6-16 
100%), moderate (33.3-66.6%), or low (0-33.3%) concordance. Cell states and Cell Ontology term diversity 17 
were analysed across all predictions. 18

generated description embeddings and precomputed Cell Ontology embeddings. Semantic similarity between 23

    "# CyteOnto\n",
    "\n",
    "Semantic Cell Type Annotation Comparison Using Large Language Models and Cell Ontology\n",
    "\n",
    "## Advanced tutorial\n",
    "\n",
    "This notebook demonstrates advanced usage of CyteOnto for semantic cell type annotation comparison, including custom embedding generation and ...\n"

  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",

   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "### Prerequisites\n",
    "\n",
    "Before you begin, ensure you have the following:\n",
    "\n",
    "- Python 3.12+\n",
    "- UV package manager (recommended)\n",
    "\n",
    "Navigate to `CyteOnto` directory and install the required packages:\n",
    "\n",
    "```bash\n",
    "uv sync\n",
    "```"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "id": "f5cbc80c",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "### 1. Set API Keys as Environment Variables\n",
    " \n",
    "```bash\n",
    "LLM_API_KEY=your_api_key_here               # For example OpenAI (can be other like groq, openrouter, google, xai, deepinfra, etc.)\n",
    "EMBEDDING_MODEL_API_KEY=your_api_key_here   # Cane be same as above if embedding model is from the same provider\n",
    " \n",
    "# Optional: for higher rate limits\n",
    "NCBI_API_KEY=your_ncbi_api_key_here         # for using pubmed tool calls\n",
    "```"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 3,
   "id": "f023e07c",
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [],
   "source": [
    "# Path management, only for running `cyteonto` from notebooks directory\n",

   "outputs": [],
   "source": [
    "import os\n",
    "\n",
    "from pydantic_ai import Agent\n",
    "from pydantic_ai.models.openai import OpenAIModel\n",
    "from pydantic_ai.providers.openai import OpenAIProvider\n"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "id": "6120188d",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "You can check out [Pydantic AI's Model Documentation](https://ai.pydantic.dev/models/) for more information on how to initialize agents using various model providers such as `OpenAI`, `Anthropic`, `Gemini`, `Groq`, `Mistral`, etc.\n",
    "\n",
    "In addition, many providers are compatible with the OpenAI API, and can be used with `OpenAIModel` in Pydantic AI: `DeepSeek`, `Grok (xAI)`, `Ollama` (for locally hosted models), etc.\n",
    "\n",
    "We will use `OpenAIModel` for our initialization of a `moonshotai/Kimi-K2-Instruct` model from `deepinfra` as an agent. The `OpenAIProvider` is used to provide the openai compatible endpoint for `deepinfra`."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 5,
   "id": "c5c6c988",
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [],
   "source": [
    "model = OpenAIModel(\n",
    "    \"moonshotai/Kimi-K2-Instruct\",\n",
    "    provider=OpenAIProvider(\n",
    "        base_url=\"https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai\",\n",
    "        api_key=os.getenv(\"LLM_API_KEY\"),\n",
    "    ),\n",
    ")\n",
    "agent = Agent(model)"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "id": "d62909bf",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "### 2. Generate Embeddings \n",
    "\n",
    "You can generate the descriptions and embeddings for Cell Ontology for using your preferred model by calling the `cyteonto.setup` function. You will need to provide the `embedding_model` and `embedding_provider` parameters to the `cyteonto.setup` function. Currenly, only `deepinfra`, `ollama`, `openai`, and `google` are supported as providers.\n",
    "\n",
    "This is a one time operation that will create the necessary embeddings for your ontology at `cyteonto/data/embedding`. For more information on managing locations, you can refer to the [`docs/FILE_MANAGEMENT.md`](../docs/FILE_MANAGEMENT.md) documentation."
   ]
  },

   "id": "f0015b40",
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [],

   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## Troubleshooting\n",
    "\n",
    "### Common Issues\n",
    "\n",
    "#### Setup Fails with Description Errors\n",
    "```bash\n",
    "# Error: Description Error: 'data'\n",
    "```\n",
    "**Solution**: Ensure you're using compatible model versions and check API connectivity.\n",
    "\n",
    "#### ParseError during Setup\n",
    "```bash\n",
    "# Error: ParseError: syntax error: line 1, column 0\n",
    "```\n",
    "**Solution**: The LLM is not returning valid JSON. Try a different model or check your API configuration.\n",
    "\n",
    "#### Connection Errors\n",
    "```bash\n",

    "```\n",
